query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, a controlled thermal aging treatment activates Mg diffusion that drives its segregation into grain boundaries and the formation of discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. This microstructural evolution modifies the surface chemistry so that, upon subsequent exposure to high-temperature oxidation and corrosive environments, a more protective MgO-enriched oxide layer forms, thereby improving both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation performance relative to the as‐cast homogeneous state.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, non-equilibrium lightweight high-entropy alloy (density below 6 g/cm³) exhibiting a homogeneous, metastable solid solution with dispersed early-stage phase features.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled thermal aging treatment designed to activate diffusion without reaching full equilibrium.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under controlled atmospheric conditions (initially inert or low-oxygen during aging, followed by standardized high-temperature oxidation and corrosion tests) with defined temperatures and durations that favor diffusion-driven segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of discrete, Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates along grain boundaries and at near-surface regions.
generation.mechanism: Thermal energy enables Mg atoms to diffusively segregate from the homogeneous solid solution, thereby nucleating and growing Mg-rich intermetallic phases. These phases alter the local chemical environment, which in turn promotes the formation of a continuous, MgO-enriched oxide layer during subsequent high-temperature oxidation. The presence of such an oxide barrier and the modified microstructure affect local electrochemical interactions, ultimately enhancing corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline as-cast state, thermally aged samples will exhibit (1) detectable formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates by XRD/SEM analysis, (2) an oxide scale with increased MgO content and improved coherency as revealed by surface analyses (e.g., XPS), and (3) lowered corrosion current densities and reduced oxidation weight gain.
generation.baseline: The initial as-cast, metastable microstructure characterized by a largely homogeneous distribution of elements without pronounced Mg segregation or intermetallic precipitates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to lightweight high-entropy alloys (density <6 g/cm³) whose compositions are prone to form both a high-entropy phase and intermetallic compounds when subjected to controlled thermal aging; deviations in alloy composition or processing conditions may lead to alternative evolution pathways.
generation.uncertainty: The extent of improvement in oxidation and corrosion resistance may vary depending on the specific thermal treatment parameters and alloy compositions, and precise quantitative changes remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one retained in the as-cast (baseline) state and the other subjected to the controlled thermal aging treatment. After treatment, expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation and standardized corrosive environments. Compare phase evolution, oxide scale composition, and corrosion behavior.
measurements: XRD and SEM/EDS to determine the formation and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates
XPS or similar surface analyses to assess the oxide scale composition and integrity
Electrochemical tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization or impedance spectroscopy) to measure corrosion rates
Weight gain measurements during high-temperature oxidation tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not result in the measurable formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates or if there is no significant improvement in the protective quality of the oxide scale as well as in corrosion resistance when compared to the as-cast baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, controlled thermal exposure drives a microstructural transition where Mg segregates into grain boundaries and forms Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. This phase evolution in turn alters the local oxidation kinetics, creating a modified oxide layer that changes the alloy’s corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior relative to the as-cast state.
drafts.material_initial_state: An as-cast, non-equilibrium solid solution alloy (e.g., Al–Mg–Cu–Zn–Gd or AlMgₓTiSnZn) with a relatively homogeneous elemental distribution and a metastable microstructure below a density of 6 g/cm³.
drafts.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to controlled thermal aging (heat treatment) under high-temperature conditions that favor diffusion and phase segregation.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert/nearly inert atmospheres with defined corrosive environments (e.g., saline solution for corrosion tests) and high-temperature oxidation conditions in a laboratory furnace. The conditions are maintained below the density limit of 6 g/cm³ and consistent with the expected diffusion regimes.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds (precipitates) at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
drafts.mechanism: Thermal energy activates diffusion processes that cause Mg to segregate and form intermetallic precipitates. The emergence of these precipitates modulates the local chemical environment, leading to selective oxidation (especially of Mg) and the formation of a modified, possibly denser and less permeable, oxide layer. This altered oxide barrier influences both the corrosion behavior via galvanic coupling differences and the high-temperature oxidation resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the initial as-cast state, thermally aged alloys will show a measurable change in phase composition (increased Mg-rich intermetallics), a distinct oxide layer (with a higher proportion of Mg oxides), and corresponding differences in corrosion rates and high-temperature oxidation performance. The corrosion response may initially be more aggressive due to galvanic effects but ultimately could transition to improved protection if the oxide layer becomes more uniform and adherent.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast, non-equilibrium microstructure of the Mg-containing alloy.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under laboratory-controlled conditions: high-temperature aging at set durations, controlled atmospheres, and standardized corrosion/oxidation tests. Observations are restricted to environments replicating high-temperature oxidation and controlled immersion tests for corrosion.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one in the as-cast state (baseline) and one subjected to controlled thermal aging. Characterize both sets using techniques such as X-ray diffraction (phase identification), scanning electron microscopy (microstructural analysis), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (oxide layer composition). Follow these with standardized corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., weight gain measurements under controlled oxygen atmosphere).
measurements: Phase constituents via XRD
Microstructural characterization and intermetallic phase distribution via SEM/EDS
Oxide layer composition via XPS
Corrosion rate via electrochemical testing
Weight change during oxidation tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not lead to the formation of distinct Mg-rich intermetallic phases, nor produce correlated changes in oxide layer composition and corresponding differences in corrosion/oxidation performance compared to the as-cast state, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In the non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, the metastable microstructure evolves under high-temperature oxidation and corrosive conditions to form Mg-enriched intermetallic compounds and/or protective MgO phases, thereby altering its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior compared to its initial state.
drafts.material_initial_state: A metastable, non-equilibrium microstructure comprising a mix of solid solutions and early-stage intermetallic compounds in an alloy with density below 6 g/cm³.
drafts.intervention: Exposure to controlled high-temperature oxidation cycles and corrosive environments (e.g., salt-spray testing).
drafts.conditions: Experiments performed at moderate high temperatures (approximately 400–600 °C) and under standardized corrosive conditions for a defined duration.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of Mg-enriched intermetallic compounds and/or a continuous MgO scale.
drafts.mechanism: Under high-temperature and oxidative conditions, the metastable alloy undergoes phase separation where Mg diffuses to nucleation sites, leading to the stabilization of Mg-rich intermetallic phases and/or formation of a protective MgO layer. This transformation alters the alloy's surface passivation, thereby improving its resistance to corrosion and high-temperature oxidation relative to its initial state.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the initial metastable condition, the evolved alloy should exhibit lower corrosion current densities and decreased oxidation weight gain due to the formation of protective intermetallic and oxide phases.
drafts.baseline: The initial alloy state is characterized by a homogeneously distributed metastable phase mixture of solid solutions and dispersed early intermetallic compounds before significant exposure to thermal or oxidative stress.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under conditions where the alloy is exposed to temperatures near 400–600 °C and standardized corrosive environments; deviations in temperature, exposure time, or environmental aggressiveness may result in alternative phase evolution pathways that do not exhibit the predicted improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare alloy samples with the specified initial metastable microstructure and subject them to controlled high-temperature oxidation (400–600 °C) and standardized salt-spray corrosion tests. Characterize the phase evolution using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and measure corrosion behavior through potentiodynamic polarization. Compare these results to control samples maintained at room temperature under inert conditions.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification via XRD
Surface morphology and intermetallic formation analysis via SEM
Corrosion current density measurements via potentiodynamic polarization testing
Oxidation weight gain measurements over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after the intervention, there is no significant formation of Mg-enriched intermetallic compounds or protective MgO phases, and if the corrosion and oxidation performance of the evolved alloy is comparable to or worse than that of the initial baseline state, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium, Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, metastable solute clusters (especially involving Mg) form during rapid processing and then evolve during subsequent thermal exposure into discrete intermetallic precipitates. This transformation changes the surface chemistry such that the evolved microstructure promotes the formation of passivating intermetallic oxides that improve corrosion resistance while simultaneously generating less protective high-temperature oxide scales that accelerate oxidation.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast, non-equilibrium Mg-containing high-entropy alloy with a predominantly metastable solid solution and dispersed solute clusters.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled aging/thermal treatment designed to promote the diffusion and precipitation of metastable clusters into stable intermetallic phases.
drafts.conditions: Aging at moderate temperatures under inert atmosphere followed by exposure to corrosive environments (e.g., NaCl solution) and high-temperature oxidation tests in ambient air (or controlled oxygen partial pressures).
drafts.structural_mediator: The evolution of metastable Mg-rich solute clusters into intermetallic precipitates that modify local composition and interfacial properties at the alloy surface.
drafts.mechanism: Rapid solidification creates a non-equilibrium, metastable solute distribution. With subsequent aging, diffusion leads to the nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds that alter the alloy’s electrochemical behavior. In corrosive media, fine, well-dispersed intermetallic phases facilitate the formation of a passivating oxide layer, while under high-temperature oxidation conditions the heterogeneous oxide scale forms an uneven and less protective barrier.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial as-cast state, aged alloys will show improved corrosion resistance (suggesting lower corrosion rates) due to a more uniform passivating layer, but will exhibit diminished high-temperature oxidation resistance (indicated by a thicker or less protective oxide scale).
drafts.baseline: As-cast, non-equilibrium alloy state with metastable solid solution and no significant intermetallic precipitates.
drafts.boundary: Lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm3 where constituent property differences predispose the material toward intermetallic compound formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy specimens: one set retains the as-cast, non-equilibrium structure; the other undergoes controlled aging designed to induce the transformation of solute clusters into intermetallic precipitates. Subject both sets to identical corrosion tests (e.g., immersion in a NaCl solution) and high-temperature oxidation tests under controlled oxygen partial pressure.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion rate (e.g., via potentiodynamic polarization or electrochemical impedance spectroscopy)
Surface oxide scale thickness and composition (e.g., via XPS, SEM/EDS, or TEM)
Phase distribution and microstructural evolution (e.g., via X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged specimens do not show a significant decrease in corrosion rate compared to the as-cast specimens, or if they do not exhibit a measurable change in high-temperature oxidation behavior (or if the trend is opposite to the predicted outcome), then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, diffusion-driven segregation during post-processing (such as controlled thermal treatment) leads to the formation of localized Mg-rich intermetallic domains. These domains, which form at grain boundaries and on surfaces, promote the preferential formation of a protective MgO layer during high-temperature oxidation while also modifying local electrochemical properties that affect corrosion behavior.
drafts.material_initial_state: An as-cast Mg-containing high-entropy alloy (e.g., MgAlCuZnGd or similar) with a homogeneous high-entropy phase and metastable interface structures, having a density below 6 g/cm3.
drafts.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal annealing treatment that is sufficient to promote diffusion-driven elemental segregation without causing full equilibrium.
drafts.conditions: Conduct experiments under controlled atmospheric conditions (inert atmosphere during aging and oxidative conditions at high temperature) and maintain consistent time intervals to allow measurable phase evolution.
drafts.structural_mediator: The evolution of discrete Mg-rich intermetallic domains along grain boundaries and near the surface.
drafts.mechanism: Thermal activation promotes diffusion of Mg, which segregates to specific microstructural regions. These segregated Mg-rich domains have a lower local stability against oxidation, leading to preferential formation of a continuous MgO layer during high-temperature exposure. The presence and connectivity of these phases also modulate localized electrochemical potentials, thereby altering the corrosion behavior relative to the initial homogeneous state.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, thermally annealed samples will display (1) XRD and microscopic evidence for emerging Mg-rich intermetallic phases, (2) a more cohesive and possibly thicker MgO surface layer that improves high-temperature oxidation resistance, and (3) measurable changes in corrosion rates due to altered local electrochemical properties at the phase boundaries.
drafts.baseline: The initial as-cast microstructure featuring a high-entropy solid solution with no significant elemental segregation or distinct Mg-rich phases.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm3 and compositions prone to forming both solid solution phases and intermetallic compounds, under controlled laboratory conditions. Results may vary if alloy compositions or processing conditions deviate significantly from those assumed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two comparative sets of the alloy: one in the as-cast (baseline) condition and one subjected to controlled thermal annealing. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation and accelerated corrosion environments. Characterize phase evolution using XRD and SEM/EDS while measuring the formation and morphology of the protective oxide layers, along with corrosion rate analysis (e.g., via electrochemical testing).
measurements: XRD for identifying phase changes and the emergence of Mg-rich intermetallics
SEM/EDS mapping to visualize and quantify segregation of Mg at grain boundaries and surfaces
Oxidation scale thickness measurements (optical or electron microscopy)
Electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization or impedance spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal annealing does not result in detectable Mg-rich intermetallic domain formation, or if no significant differences in high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion behavior are observed between the annealed and the as-cast samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
